analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to sell prescriptions to Medicare beneficiaries' pharmacies at the government's lowest price.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut Medicare beneficiaries' drug prices by an estimated 40 percent was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in March 1999 and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drug manufacturers that sell to the federal government to also sell to pharmacies, at the government's lowest price, whatever amount those pharmacies needed to serve Medicare beneficiaries. Medicare patients at the time paid about twice as much as the government's most favored customers for the same drugs, and the bill's findings estimated prices would fall by more than 40 percent. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 39 million Medicare beneficiaries who bought their own prescription drugs would gain, according to the bill's own findings: they paid about twice as much as the drug makers' most favored customers, and some paid more than 15 times as much. The bill would extend the lowest federal price to retail pharmacies serving Medicare patients, which the bill's findings estimate would cut those prices by more than 40 percent. Hospice patients would also be covered [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries paying cash for prescriptions

how_it_helps.text: It would cut what Medicare beneficiaries pay out of pocket for prescriptions by extending the lowest price the federal government already pays for the same drugs, which the bill's findings estimate would reduce prices by more than 40 percent [S2][S3].
It would end the price gap in which seniors paying cash for drugs could pay more than 15 times what health insurers or federal programs pay for the same drug [S3].
It would include drugs furnished to terminally ill Medicare patients in hospice programs, extending the lower prices to some of the sickest beneficiaries [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers that sell drugs to the federal government would bear the cost, since they would be required to sell to pharmacies at the government's lowest price or their best price, whichever is lower, cutting the margins they earn on drugs sold to Medicare beneficiaries [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would be a government-mandated price control: it ties manufacturers' ability to contract with the federal government to selling all Medicare-bound drugs at the government's lowest price, which drug makers argued would reduce revenue available for developing new medicines.

The 'best price' mechanism, borrowed from Medicaid, was widely criticized at the time for producing artificially low reported prices and distorting discounts, so its use as a pricing benchmark could have produced unintended effects on the broader drug market.
The bill does not create a Medicare drug benefit; it relies on pharmacies buying at the mandated price and does not address how beneficiaries would actually obtain or pay for coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is large and concrete: millions of seniors paying cash for prescriptions would have seen prices drop by an estimated 40 percent or more, easing documented hardship where seniors skip medicine or food [S3]. The cost falls on a single concentrated group, drug manufacturers that contract with the government, and the strongest honest objection is that mandated price floors could reduce drug-industry revenue for research. That trade-off was never tested in debate, because the committee never took the bill up at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee in March 1999 and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 25, 1999 by Sen. Kennedy with 8 original cosponsors and read twice before being referred to the Senate Finance Committee [S1][S3][S5].

The bill's findings state that older Americans who buy their own drugs pay on average twice as much as the drug makers' most favored customers, and that more than 1 in 8 sometimes choose between food and medicine [S3].
After the referral to Finance, the record shows no further action of any kind for the remainder of the 106th Congress, which ended January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries who buy their own prescriptions gained nothing; drug manufacturers kept the ability to charge seniors roughly twice what their most favored customers pay, a pricing structure the bill's findings valued at about $20 billion a year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug manufacturers kept their pricing freedom

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 11 Democratic cosponsors

against.name: Committee leadership of the Senate Finance Committee (chaired by Sen. William Roth)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Brand-name drug manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending the government's lowest drug prices to all Medicare beneficiaries during this era of drug-pricing debates

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 12 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never moved in the Republican-led Senate Finance Committee; no vote was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would force any manufacturer selling to the U.S. government to extend its lowest federal price or its 'best price' to pharmacies serving Medicare beneficiaries, directly cutting into the roughly $20 billion in annual profits the bill's findings attribute to differential pricing. By never advancing, the bill left that pricing structure untouched.
Pharmacies would have been able to buy drugs for Medicare patients at the government's lowest price and pass the savings on; the bill changes their supplier terms but not their dispensing role.
